before.label: Jacques Lacan
before.description: Reworks psychoanalysis using language and symbolic relations. The divided subject challenges the idea of a fully self-transparent individual.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Freud is a fundamental antecedent; Saussure, Jakobson, and Lévi-Strauss inform Lacan’s approach. Écrits (1966).

after.label: Jacques Lacan
after.description: Rereads Freud through identification, language and symbolic relations. The mirror-stage argument explains ego unity through an external image; later work recasts dream condensation and displacement through metaphor and metonymy. His divided subject becomes a resource and a problem for historical accounts of gender.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Freud is a fundamental antecedent; Saussure, Jakobson, and Lévi-Strauss inform Lacan’s approach. Écrits (1966).
after.scope_note: Individual thinker, not a uniform school. The 1949 mirror-stage paper, 1953 report first published in 1956, 1957 linguistic essay and 1966 Écrits collection are distinct witnesses. Saussure’s diagram is transformed, Jakobson explicitly credited, and Lévi-Strauss named as a resource. Althusser appropriates his reading of Freud; Scott finds constructed subjectivity instructive but questions universal sexual antagonism and limited historical variability. These are situated theoretical arguments, not independently established clinical or developmental facts. Later seminars and revisions remain outside this bounded primary reading.

before.label: Louis Althusser
before.description: Reinterprets Marx through structural causality, overdetermination, and a critique of humanism. Generates sharp disputes about historical explanation and agency.
before.representative_figures_and_works: For Marx and Reading Capital (1965). E. P. Thompson’s The Poverty of Theory (1978) directly attacks his approach.

after.label: Louis Althusser
after.description: Reinterprets Marx through problematics, an epistemological break and overdetermined contradictions. Political and ideological circumstances have explanatory force; material institutions and practices constitute subjects while remaining sites of class struggle. Collective reading, later qualifications and disputes over evidence and agency shape the program.
after.representative_figures_and_works: For Marx and Reading Capital (1965). E. P. Thompson’s The Poverty of Theory (1978) directly attacks his approach.
after.scope_note: Individual thinker whose positions change; neither all Marxism nor a timeless structuralist system. For Marx and the five-author Reading Capital appeared in 1965; the consulted revised abridgment omits three contributors and acknowledges a unilateral theoreticism. Bachelard, Martin, Canguilhem, Cavaillès, Foucault, Lacan and Gramsci supply named resources with different evidential scopes. Thompson’s criticism and Hall’s productive disagreement are distinct interventions. Interpellation is a theoretical illustration, not a chronological experiment; apparatuses also involve resistance and struggle beyond institutions. Later political revisions and other collaborators’ original chapters remain bounded research limits.

before.label: Historical epistemology

strands.title: Development, transference and sublimation
strands.focus: Freud’s sexuality extends beyond reproduction; transference and sublimation connect his developmental and clinical account. Its normative sexual classifications are historical judgments.

strands.title: Individual relations and group bonds
strands.focus: Group Psychology starts with relations already present in individual life and questions suggestion as a sufficient explanation, proposing libidinal attachments.

strands.title: Child analysis and divergent developments
strands.focus: Klein’s play interpretation differs from other early child-analysis practices. Anna Freud and Klein are not interchangeable extensions of Freud; support here is a retrospective institutional profile.

strands.title: Psychosocial and historical adaptations
strands.focus: Erikson examines identity in historical orders; Gay argues for a place within contextual history. Neither position represents all psychoanalytic traditions.

strands.title: Feminist questions and subjectivity

strands.works: Psychoanalysis and Feminism (1974); Becoming a Woman (1994/1995)

strands.title: Translation, context and historical inference
strands.focus: Schapiro’s Leonardo criticism tests an application against historical knowledge while retaining the possibility of psychological inquiry. Unrecorded motives are not directly accessible clinical facts.
